A tautology is a statement that says the same thing twice — just using different words — without adding any new information. The second part of the statement doesn't teach you anything you didn't already know from the first part. It just restates it.

The word has two closely related but distinct meanings depending on whether you're talking about everyday language or formal logic. Both are important.

This is the most common way people use the word. A tautology in everyday language is a phrase or sentence where you repeat an idea unnecessarily, because the meaning is already fully contained in the first part.

Simple examples:

  • "A free gift" — A gift is, by definition, something given for free. Saying "free" adds nothing.
  • "The end result" — A result is always something that comes at the end. "End" is redundant.
  • "I saw it with my own eyes" — You can't see things with someone else's eyes. "My own" adds nothing.
  • "Return back" — To return already means to go back. "Back" is unnecessary.
  • "Join together" — To join already means to come together.
  • "A new innovation" — An innovation is always new by definition.
  • "Unexpected surprise" — A surprise is always unexpected.

In every case, if you remove the repeated part, the sentence still means exactly the same thing. The extra word or phrase was dead weight.

Why it matters in writing: Tautologies are generally considered a weakness in writing. They make your language bloated and imprecise. A careful writer avoids them because every word should earn its place.

Ask yourself: "If I remove this word or phrase, does the sentence lose any meaning?"

If the answer is no — if the meaning is fully intact without it — then what you removed was a tautology.

For example: "The murdered victim was killed."

  • "Murdered" already means killed. Saying "was killed" repeats the same idea.
  • You could just say "The victim was murdered" or "The victim was killed." Both are complete.
When Tautologies Are Intentional (Not Always a Mistake)

Sometimes people use tautologies deliberately — not out of carelessness, but for effect. These are sometimes called rhetorical tautologies, and they appear constantly in everyday speech.

  • "It is what it is."
  • "Boys will be boys."
  • "A deal is a deal."
  • "War is war."

Logically, these sentences say nothing new — of course a thing is what it is. But their purpose isn't to inform; it's to express an attitude, like resignation, acceptance, or firmness. People understand exactly what you mean when you say them. So while they are technically tautologies, they serve a communicative function through tone and implication.

The key difference: an unintentional tautology is a flaw. An intentional one can be a stylistic choice.
Meaning 2: In Formal Logic and Philosophy

In logic, the word "tautology" has a more precise and technical meaning. Here, a tautology is a statement that is always and necessarily true — not because of facts about the world, but purely because of how it is constructed.

No matter what happens in reality, a logical tautology cannot be false.

Examples:

  • "It will either rain tomorrow or it won't rain tomorrow."
    This must be true. There is no third option. Its truth has nothing to do with the actual weather.
  • "She is either at home or she is not at home."
    Again, always true by necessity, in any circumstance.
  • "All bachelors are unmarried."
    This is true not because of any fact you looked up — it's true because "bachelor" is defined as an unmarried man. It couldn't be otherwise.

The key feature: a logical tautology tells you nothing about the real world because it's true in every possible world. It carries zero information about reality — it's true regardless of facts.

Is this good or bad in logic? Unlike in writing, tautologies in logic are actually important and useful. They are the bedrock of logical proofs and mathematical reasoning. Identifying that something is a tautology confirms it is an airtight, unbreakable truth within a logical system.

It's worth noting that a tautology is not just any kind of repetition. If you say "The dog is a dog," that's a tautology. But if you say "The dog barked and barked," that's just repetition for emphasis — it's not a tautology, because both uses of "barked" refer to the same action, not the same meaning being stated twice.

A tautology is specifically about meaning being duplicated, not words being repeated.

ContextWhat it means

In everyday language, a tautology is a phrase that says the same thing twice without adding meaning — like "free gift" or "end result." It's usually a writing flaw, though sometimes intentional for rhetorical effect.

In formal logic, a tautology is a statement that is always necessarily true by its own structure, no matter what — like "it will either rain or it won't." It carries no information about reality but is logically unbreakable.

Both meanings share the same underlying idea: something that adds no new information, because the truth of it is already fully contained within itself.
